## Recommended Data Sets






## Problematic Data Sets

We **do not support** the use of the following data sets in teaching or research: 

### "Pima Indians" (Akimel O'odham) Data Set

The "Pima Indians" data set has been openly provided by the [UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/) and is accessible through code-based platforms like [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/) and various R packages ([mlbench](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mlbench/index.html), [faraway](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/faraway/index.html), and [pdp](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pdp/index.html), to name a few). It is a data set that is commonly used to demonstrate the use of predictive modelling for diabetes mellitus. The use of this data set is prevalent in both teaching and research. 

The Indigenous Peoples whose data are recorded in this data set refer to themselves as **Akimel O'odham**, which translates to *River People* [@radin2017digital]. They reside in the Gila River Indian Community outisde of Phoenix, Arizona. The ancestors of the Akimel O'odham, HuHuKam, are known for their agricultural innovations [@radin2017digital]. They drew upon the Gila River and created irrigation infrastructure to support their agriculture [@radin2017digital]. This community saw a lot of hardship in the 1800s, including disruptions due to the California gold rush and the construction of dams and other structures from non-Native farmers that greatly impacted water sources for the Indigenous Peoples along the Gila River [@radin2017digital]. 

In 1901, anthropologist Frank Russell came to the Gila River for a study. Posthumous, his work entitled "The Pima" was published. The community members did not have control of the cultural descriptions and verbiage used in Russell's work [@radin2017digital]. He also noted in a letter to his boss in 1902 that "these people are starving so that I am getting specimens and information that would otherwise not be attainable" [@radin2017digital]. The community experienced mass famine and starvation, which caused the American government to supply canned and processed food assistance between 1908 and 1955. Prior to this food assistance, only one case of diabetes was reported in the population [@radin2017digital]. Then, in 1990, the Gila River Community had "the highest recorded prevalence and incidence of non-insulin dependent diabetes of any geographically defined population" [@radin2017digital]. Community members have noted that the rise of obesity and Type 2 diabetes coincides with their loss of ability to farm their land and the change of diet introduced by the American government [@radin2017digital]. 

Prior to the rise of modern genomics and epidemiology, the data collected on the Akimel O'odham were a valuable resource for diabetes research and knowledge [@radin2017digital]. This data were eventually translated into digital forms, which enabled it to be used more widely in research. This included research that was not related to diabetes [@radin2017digital].
